title: Computational models of causal judgment
text: Computing causal judgment requires three steps: -Specify causal model, -Specify happened actual world, -Request causal judgment. example, suppose variable E happens B happen. specify causal model : string '&b' specifies structural equation E. numbers .1 .9 exogenous probabilities B. Next must specify happens actual world: says actual world, variables value 1. .e. happened, B happened, E happened. Finally request causal judgment: first two arguments say want see extent caused E. next two arguments specify causal model actual-world value variables (defined ). fifth argument specifies computational model want use (, CES). last argument specifies value stability parameter ss (much counterfactual simulation ‘anchored’ actual world). argument optional, default s=0s=0. Running command return ‘causal score’ -1 1 (CES) 0 1 (NS). Higher values indicate higher actual causal strength. CES model, negative value like -.8 indicates weak causal score, something like ‘negative’ causation. -.8 weaker example -.4. examples provided vignette. References: Icard, Kominsky & Knobe (2017). Normality actual causal strength. Cognition. Quillien & Lucas (2023). Counterfactuals logic causal selection. Psychological Review.

what: This helper function computes the value of Y conditioned on a counterfactual intervention on X, starting from a given world. We will use that function for computing both necessity and sufficiency. This function works recursively. Suppose Y depends directly on X: then the function can directly compute the effect of the intervention. But Y can also indirectly depend on X, for example via a chain X -> Z -> Y. To accommodate this kind of cases, we recursively call the compute_counterfactual_value() function on intermediate values, until we reach X. — compute_counterfactual_value
